items.title: AI and your job: Threat or opportunity?
items.summary:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA) - Artificial intelligence is becoming a bigger part of everyday life, raising questions about what the technology could mean for workers and their jobs.

Some economists believe AI poses a particular threat to entry-level and repetitive work, including call center, data entry and junior copywriting jobs, according to The Wall Street Journal. Those tasks may be easier to automate. [...] But AI could also create opportunities. A Bloomberg article points to potential job growth in construction and manufacturing as companies build data centers and produce the chips that power the technology. Some higher-skilled office workers could also benefit if AI helps them become more productive. [...] The long-term impact on jobs remains unclear, but workers can take steps to prepare. Exploring AI chatbots, writing assistants and other tools may help people find ways to work more efficiently and develop skills that complement the technology.

items.title: Opinion: AI cannot replace being human – The Battalion
items.summary: I understand the appeal. College is busy. Between classes, jobs, extracurriculars, leadership positions and trying to maintain some semblance of a social life, there are never enough hours in the day. AI makes things easier. It can generate an outline, rewrite a paragraph, summarize a reading or produce an entire essay before you have even finished your Celsius. But convenience does not necessarily facilitate education. [...] There is also something to be said about individuality. AI can generate an argument, imitate a writing style or suggest a creative direction, but our perspectives are developed through our own experiences, disagreements, mistakes and interpretations. The things that make our voices interesting are often the very things that cannot be neatly generated from a prompt. If we constantly rely on the same tools to tell us what to think and how to express it, we risk losing the differences that make [...] I am not asking anyone to abandon AI. I use it, and I recognize the benefits it provides. But I do think we need to become more conscientious about when we use it and what we are asking it to do for us. Let it help with the tedious tasks. Let it serve as a resource. But do not let it become a substitute for your own intellectual development.

items.title: 5/5 🧵 My analysis
items.summary:
5/5 🧵 My analysis
The result that caught my attention most is the improvement from 40% to 95% average task success with only five demonstrations per task.

In industrial robotics, teleoperating a robot to collect training data for every new product or workstation takes time.
If similar adaptation results can be reproduced across different robots and real factory environments, preparing robots for new tasks could require far fewer recorded demonstrations.

There is also a practical advantage.

Videos of humans performing manual tasks are far more abundant than recordings collected directly from robots.

That gives GR00T 2 access to a much larger source of training data.

The next test will be whether these results hold across unfamiliar objects, changing environments and long industrial operating cycles.

Official NVIDIA research:
https://t.co/04yiGMCaeh

items.title: 3/5 🧵 Why this is useful for robotics
items.summary:
3/5 🧵 Why this is useful for robotics
GR00T 2 has four practical advantages:

• Human video learning: Robots can acquire certain skills from people performing tasks without requiring demonstrations of every task on the target robot.

• Fast adaptation: Five demonstrations and around 30 minutes of fine-tuning were enough to reach 95% average success in NVIDIA's evaluation.

• Cross-robot transfer: Skills learned from handheld demonstration devices can be adapted to robotic arms and five-fingered hands.

• AI agent coordination: A reasoning model can organize task steps, monitor progress and initiate recovery procedures when something goes wrong.

NVIDIA also combined GR00T 2 with a reasoning agent on a YAM robotic arm.
The system successfully completed 292 out of 300 assembly attempts across three different toys.

items.title: Fable 5.2 more than DOUBLED its robotics score in one release...
items.summary:
Fable 5.2 more than DOUBLED its robotics score in one release...

RoboDojo Sim:
> Fable 5.2: 64.9%
> Opus 5.5: 39.4%
> Fable 5.1: 27.6%

trust benchmarks or not, a jump this big shows you what they're training their models for next

luckily it's not too late to get ahead:

1. AI, the whole way through
have Claude or Codex explain every schematic, write your firmware and debug with you
there's no learning robotics without AI anymore, and anyone telling you otherwise isn't looking even two years ahead

2. electronics, for free
learn Ohm's law, voltage dividers and transistor switches in Falstad or Tinkercad before you spend a dollar
a lot of robot bugs are electrical, a loose wire or a motor pulling more current than your board can supply, and you can't fix what you don't understand

3. microcontrollers and motors
start on Arduino because every tutorial targets it, then move to an ESP32 for WiFi and more power
use a TB6612FNG or DRV8833 motor driver, the L298N in every tutorial is obsolete and wastes your battery as heat
build a line follower, then a self-balancing robot, and use millis() instead of delay() or your timing will fall apart

4. CAD and 3D printing
pick one tool, Onshape or Fusion, and design parts from the datasheets of the hardware you own
print a tolerance gauge first so you know your printer's clearances, and use PETG for anything that has to survive a drop

5. an open-source robot arm
the SO-101 from Hugging Face and TheRobotStudio comes as a leader and follower pair, you move one by hand and the other copies it
that setup is how you'll record training data later

6. ROS 2 and simulation
learn ROS 2 Jazzy with Gazebo Harmonic, then SLAM Toolbox and Nav2, all on a normal laptop with no GPU
if a tutorial says catkin_make or roscore, it's ROS 1, which is end of life, so close the tab

7. the math underneath
PID first, then kinematics from Kevin Lynch's Modern Robotics, which is free online
for balancing, a complementary filter is a few lines and works long before you need a Kalman filter

8. robot learning
LeRobot's loop is teleoperate, record, train, deploy, and ACT is the policy to start with
record around 50 demos of one task, then record more of whatever it fails at and retrain
SmolVLA is built for cheap hardware like the SO-101, so fine-tune that before reaching for a 7B model

9. content
film every build and post it, the failures included
a clip of something you built is proof nobody can fake, and it's also how founders and companies find you nowadays
